Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Rowdy Partners 1.1 Gameplay Flow 1.2 Rules of the Trick 1.3 Damage and the Pin Zone 1.4 Pop System and Tokens 1.5 Game Variants (Headliners) 1.6 Player Decisions and Strategy Rowdy Partners Rowdy Partners is a team-based trick-taking game in a wrestling setting. The goal is to "pin" an opponent by reducing their health to the final skull space on their tracker. Rowdy Partners has 4 suits (Hats, Horsehoes, Stars, and Tombstones of values 1-8); wild cards (values 3-6) count as any suit. Gameplay Flow The game is played over several rounds. Each round consists of exactly 8 tricks . Round Structure: Each player receives 8 cards. 4 cards are set aside as the "Burn Pile." Trick Sequence: The wrestler in the #1 position leads the first card. Other players follow clockwise. Winning Condition: The game ends immediately when a wrestler's health marker reaches the skull icon. Rules of the Trick Lowest Card Wins: Unlike most trick-taking games, the lowest card of the led suit wins the trick. Following Suit: Players must follow the led suit (Hat, Horseshoe, Star, or Gravestone). If a player cannot follow suit, they may play any card ("Sloughing off"). Wildcards: These represent all suits and can be played at any time. If led, the player declares the suit. Counters: If a player plays a card with the same value as a card already in the trick, both cards are flipped over. They no longer count toward winning the trick. The next available face-up card determines the suit to be followed. Damage and the Pin Zone Dealing Damage: The winner of the trick deals damage to the opposing wrestler currently "in the ring" (Position #1 or #2). Damage equals the (potentially modified) card value. Winning the Lead: The winner of the trick moves to Position #1 and leads the next trick. Pin Zone (Stop Signs): The health track contains "Stop Signs." To pass a Stop Sign, a minimum amount of damage is required (e.g., 1+, 2+, or 3+ damage). Only one Stop Sign can be passed per trick. Excess damage is lost when a Stop Sign is hit. Pop System and Tokens Playing cards with Pop symbols advances the team on the Pop Track . Reaching specific icons grants tokens: Coin: Modify your card value up or down (can be used to trigger Counters). Damage: Deals +1 extra damage if the trick is won. Tag: Allows a player to swap positions with their partner before playing a card. Cheats: Face-down tiles providing powerful bonuses like suit changes or value shifts. Signature Move: Unlocks the wrestler’s unique special ability. Game Variants (Headliners) 2-3 Players: Players without partners play as "Headliners." Two Cards: A Headliner plays two cards per trick—one from their hand and one from a "Manager Diamond" (an open display). Position: Headliners are always considered "in the ring" and take all incoming damage. Player Decisions and Strategy Table Talk: Players are not allowed to discuss specific card values or suits in their hand. Token Timing: Tokens are typically spent during your turn when playing a card. Effects can be stacked. Modifiers: Card values can be modified above 8 or below 1. A value of 0 or less deals no damage but can still win a trick. [Rating: 1/10] Oh no, they combined trick-taking with full-blown eurogame nonsense. Boards and chits everywhere, muddying the experience into an optimization puzzle.

[Rating: 3/10] I love trick-taking games and fighting games, but unfortunately the combination of the two here does not work well. The chance of a bad draw locking the game into a forgone conclusion is just too high (even with the tokens to try to correct it). Also, the tokens end up being way to fiddley to be an enjoyable addition.  If I want a quick, fighting style game, I would rather play something like Dice Throne or Tag Team. If I want to play a trick-taking game, there are literally dozens out there that I would choose first.

[Rating: 3/10] This game only has card indexes in the upper left corner. This is an inconvenience for anybody who fans their cards the other way, and it means that you have to make sure the cards are all rotated the same way every round after cards are dealt out. If you're not going to use four-corner indexes, at least add an index to the lower right of each card so they don't have to be constantly rotated.  Another annoyance is that most of the characters are just a guy wearing a big cowboy hat. When you have to look for the tokens that match your character, it's a bit of a hassle. [Rating: 4/10] My game group are trick-taking junkies, but even if we could get past the clunkiness and fiddliness of this game, there was just not enough strategy and too much randomness to enjoy it.   The awesome wrestling theme just wasn’t enough.

[Rating: 5/10] Thought I was going love this but ended up really bouncing off it hard. The saving grace for me is I can see all the fun elements that should combine to make a wild chaotic good time but just didn’t for me. I think it might have just been my complete lack of understanding anything I was supposed to do or how you gain advantage and a repeat play might go better. As is though, very early in the year it’s my least favorite new to me game of 2026.

[Rating: 5/10] In this team based trick taking game, players are split into 2 teams. Players (team 1 player 1, then 2 players on team 2, the last player on team 1) take turns playing into a trick (must follow) and triggering token powers. Players with the same value flip their cards (out of the trick). Player with the lowest lead value wins and deals equal damage to the opponents player in the ring (there's 2 players in the ring and 2 ready to be tag teamed in).
